key_terms.meaning: D = ∂/∂x and D′ = ∂/∂y; shorthand that lets you treat a constant-coefficient PDE like a polynomial in D and D′.
Writing an operator such as D² − 3DD′ + 2D′² as (D − D′)(D − 2D′).
A first order equation like z_x − m z_y = 0 has solution z = f(y + mx); each factor contributes one such f.

key_terms.term: Discriminant of a second order PDE
key_terms.meaning: For A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G, the number Δ = B² − 4AC.
Δ = B² − 4AC < 0; example u_xx + u_yy = 0, a steady-state problem.
Δ = B² − 4AC = 0; example u_t = α² u_xx, heat conduction.
Δ = B² − 4AC > 0; example u_tt = c² u_xx, wave motion.
Curves with dy/dx = (B ± √(B² − 4AC)) / (2A); real only for hyperbolic equations.
Trial form u(x, t) = X(x) T(t) that splits a PDE into two ordinary differential equations.
The number λ with X″/X = T′/(α²T) = −λ, the only link between the two ODEs.
u_tt = c² u_xx, where c is the wave speed in m/s.
u(x, t) = ½[f(x − ct) + f(x + ct)] + (1/2c)∫ from x − ct to x + ct of g(s) ds, for an infinite string with u(x, 0) = f(x), u_t(x, 0) = g(x).
F(x − ct) moves right at speed c, G(x + ct) moves left at speed c; both keep their shape.
u_t = α² u_xx, where α² is the thermal diffusivity in m²/s.
A term e^(−α²n²π²t/L²) sin(nπx/L) whose amplitude falls exponentially with time.
u_xx + u_yy = 0, the steady state reached by both heat and wave problems.
Any solution of Laplace's equation; it has no maximum or minimum in the interior of its domain.
u_rr + (1/r)u_r + (1/r²)u_θθ = 0, the natural form inside a disk of radius a.
∫ from 0 to L of sin(nπx/L) sin(mπx/L) dx equals L/2 when n = m and 0 when n ≠ m.
b_n = (2/L)∫ from 0 to L of f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx, the weight multiplying the n-th mode.

takeaways: Constant coefficients let you factor the operator, and every first order factor gives one arbitrary function of a combined variable.
The sign of B² − 4AC decides the type: elliptic has no real characteristics, parabolic one family, hyperbolic two families.
Separation of variables turns one PDE into two ODEs joined by a single constant, and the boundary conditions pick the allowed values of that constant.
The wave equation carries the initial shape in two directions at speed c; D'Alembert's formula writes exactly that.
The heat equation damps high modes fastest, so the temperature profile flattens as time grows and only the longest mode survives.
Laplace's equation gives steady potentials: sinh and sine in a rectangle, powers r^n and cos nθ in a disk.
Fourier series are the fitting tool; orthogonality pulls out each coefficient from the initial or boundary data.
The PDE alone is not the problem; boundary and initial conditions choose which modes exist and how fast they decay.
bank_note: Long answers almost always ask for a full boundary value problem: classify the equation, separate it, find the eigenvalues, fit the data with Fourier coefficients and write the final series, so show every stage.

bank.q: Define elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic second order linear PDEs in two variables using the discriminant, and give one physical situation modelled by each.
outline: Write the general form A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G with A, B, C functions of x, y.
Define Δ = B² − 4AC and state the three sign cases.
Elliptic example u_xx + u_yy = 0: steady temperature in a plate.
Parabolic example u_t = α² u_xx: cooling of a rod.
Hyperbolic example u_tt = c² u_xx: vibration of a string.
Mention that the type is fixed by the second order terms only.

bank.q: Explain why a linear homogeneous PDE with constant coefficients is solved by factoring the operator, and why each first order factor brings an arbitrary function instead of a constant.
outline: Introduce D = ∂/∂x, D′ = ∂/∂y and treat the operator as a polynomial.
Factor the polynomial into real linear factors (D − m₁D′)(D − m₂D′)…
Solve the simplest case u_x − m u_y = 0 to get u = f(y + mx).
Point out that the 'constant' of integration now depends on the other characteristic variable, so it is an arbitrary function.
Superpose one arbitrary function per factor for the general solution.
Give one worked illustration, e.g. (D² − 3DD′ + 2D′²)z = 0 gives z = f(y + x) + g(y + 2x).

bank.q: State D'Alembert's solution for the infinite string and explain the meaning of each term.
outline: Write u_tt = c² u_xx with u(x,0) = f(x) and u_t(x,0) = g(x).
Factor as (∂/∂t − c∂/∂x)(∂/∂t + c∂/∂x)u = 0.
General solution u = F(x − ct) + G(x + ct).
Apply initial conditions to get F and G, then the integral form of the formula.
Explain: half the initial displacement travels right and half left; the integral term is the accumulated effect of the initial velocity.

bank.q: Describe the method of separation of variables for u_t = α²u_xx on 0 < x < L with both ends held at zero, and explain how the separation constant is fixed.
outline: Assume u = X(x)T(t) and substitute.
Divide by α²XT to get T′/(α²T) = X″/X = −λ.
Argue that a function of t alone can equal a function of x alone only if both are constant.
Solve X″ + λX = 0 with X(0) = X(L) = 0 to get λ = n²π²/L² and X = sin(nπx/L).
Solve T′ + α²λT = 0 to get the decaying exponential.
Superpose and fit the initial condition using a Fourier sine series.

bank.q: State the orthogonality relation for sin(nπx/L) on 0 ≤ x ≤ L and use it to obtain the Fourier sine coefficient formula.
outline: Write the integral of sin(nπx/L) sin(mπx/L) from 0 to L.
Show it is 0 for n ≠ m and L/2 for n = m.
Multiply the assumed series f(x) = Σ b_n sin(nπx/L) by sin(mπx/L) and integrate term by term.
All terms vanish except n = m, giving b_n = (2/L)∫ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.
State the condition: f must be piecewise smooth for the series to converge to f.
Factor the operator as (D − D′)(D − 2D′)z = 0.
First factor: z_x − z_y = 0 gives z = f(y + x).
Second factor: z_x − 2z_y = 0 gives z = g(y + 2x).
Add by superposition: z = f(y + x) + g(y + 2x).
State that f and g are arbitrary functions, twice differentiable.

bank.q: Solve (D² + DD′ − 6D′²)z = 0 and verify the answer by substitution.
outline: Factor: D² + DD′ − 6D′² = (D + 3D′)(D − 2D′).
Solve z_x + 3z_y = 0 to get f(y − 3x).
Solve z_x − 2z_y = 0 to get g(y + 2x).
General solution z = f(y − 3x) + g(y + 2x).
Verify: substitute back and show both second derivatives cancel.

bank.q: Classify u_xx + x u_yy = 0 at every point of the plane and describe the geometry of the three regions.
outline: Identify A = 1, B = 0, C = x.
Compute Δ = B² − 4AC = −4x.
x < 0: Δ > 0, hyperbolic, two real characteristic families.
x = 0: Δ = 0, parabolic on the whole y-axis.
x > 0: Δ < 0, elliptic.
Comment that the type is not fixed because the coefficients are not constant.

bank.q: Solve the wave equation u_tt = c²u_xx on 0 < x < L with u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0, u(x,0) = f(x) and u_t(x,0) = 0.
outline: Separate u = X(x)T(t) to get X″ + λX = 0 and T″ + c²λT = 0.
Boundary conditions force λ = n²π²/L² and X = sin(nπx/L).
Time part gives cos(nπct/L) and sin(nπct/L).
Zero initial velocity kills the sine-in-time terms.
Write u = Σ b_n cos(nπct/L) sin(nπx/L) with b_n the Fourier sine coefficients of f.
Interpret each term as a standing wave with node spacing L/n.

bank.q: A rod of length 1 m has both ends held at 0 °C and initial temperature u(x,0) = 100 sin(πx) °C, with α² = 1 m²/s. Find u(x,t) and the time at which the midpoint falls to 50 °C.
outline: Set up u_t = α²u_xx, u(0,t) = u(1,t) = 0, u(x,0) = 100 sin(πx).
General separated solution u = Σ b_n e^(−α²n²π²t/L²) sin(nπx/L) with L = 1.
The initial data is already a single sine, so only n = 1 survives and b₁ = 100.
Thus u = 100 e^(−π²t) sin(πx).
Solve: t = ln 2 / π² ≈ 0.070 s.

bank.q: Solve Laplace's equation in the rectangle 0 < x < a, 0 < y < b, with u = 0 on x = 0, x = a and y = 0, and u(x,b) = f(x).
outline: Separate u = X(x)Y(y) to get X″ + λX = 0 and Y″ − λY = 0.
Three zero conditions give λ = n²π²/a² and X = sin(nπx/a).
Y solves Y″ − (n²π²/a²)Y = 0, so use sinh(nπy/a) to satisfy Y(0) = 0.
Write u = Σ b_n sinh(nπy/a) sin(nπx/a).
Impose y = b: b_n sinh(nπb/a) are the Fourier sine coefficients of f.
So u = Σ c_n [sinh(nπy/a) / sinh(nπb/a)] sin(nπx/a), with c_n the sine coefficients of f.

bank.q: Solve Laplace's equation inside a disk of radius a with boundary value u(a,θ) = f(θ), and justify why some separated solutions are thrown away.
outline: Use polar form u_rr + (1/r)u_r + (1/r²)u_θθ = 0 with u = R(r)Θ(θ).
Θ″ + n²Θ = 0 for periodicity in θ, giving cos nθ and sin nθ with integer n.
R solves r²R″ + rR′ − n²R = 0, with solutions r^n and r^(−n).
Discard r^(−n) because the potential must be finite at r = 0; discard log r for n = 0 for the same reason.
Write u = a₀/2 + Σ r^n (a_n cos nθ + b_n sin nθ).
At r = a these are the Fourier coefficients of f(θ) on [−π, π].

bank.q: Compare the heat equation and the wave equation mode by mode, and explain why one smooths the initial data while the other preserves its shape.
outline: Both separate into the same sine modes in x with λ = n²π²/L².
Time factors: e^(−α²λt) for heat, cos(√λ ct) and sin(√λ ct) for the wave equation.
Heat amplitudes decay at a rate proportional to n², so high modes die fast and corners round off.
Wave amplitudes oscillate without decay, so the profile repeats and information travels along characteristics.
Consequence: heat solutions become smooth for any t > 0; wave solutions keep discontinuities along the lines x ± ct = constant.
Mention that only the wave equation is reversible in time.

bank.q: Explain how the type of a second order PDE with variable coefficients can change from point to point, using u_xx + x u_yy = 0, and say what this means for solving it.
outline: Compute Δ = −4x, which depends on position.
Region x < 0 hyperbolic, line x = 0 parabolic, region x > 0 elliptic.
In the hyperbolic region two real characteristic families exist and a D'Alembert-type solution is possible.
In the elliptic region there are no real characteristics; boundary value data on a closed curve is the natural problem.
On x = 0 the equation degenerates and the usual classification tools fail.
Conclude that a single global formula is not available; solutions are usually matched across the parabolic line.

bank.q: A semi-infinite string occupies x ≥ 0 with the end x = 0 fixed. Explain how D'Alembert's solution is extended to cover this case and why an odd extension is the correct choice.
outline: Start with the infinite-string formula for the odd extension of the initial data.
The fixed end demands u(0,t) = 0 for all t.
The forward wave F(x − ct) reaching x = 0 must be cancelled by a reflected wave, which the odd extension supplies.
Oddness gives f(−s) = −f(s), so the two contributions at x = 0 add to zero.
State that the reflected pulse returns inverted, as observed on a string tied at one end.
Note the same idea extends to a finite string by repeated reflections.

glossary.def: An equation involving an unknown function of two or more variables and its partial derivatives.
The order of the highest derivative appearing in the equation.
A PDE in which the unknown function and its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together.
A linear PDE with no term free of the unknown function, so the zero function is always a solution.
Any finite sum of solutions of a linear homogeneous PDE is again a solution.
A boundary condition that prescribes the value of the unknown function itself on the boundary.
A boundary condition that prescribes the normal derivative of the unknown function on the boundary.
Data given at one time level, needed because the heat and wave equations are first order in time or second order in time.
A PDE together with conditions on the boundary of the region, whose solution is sought inside the region.

glossary.term: Eigenvalue of a boundary value problem
glossary.def: A value of the separation constant for which a nonzero solution satisfying the boundary conditions exists.
The nonzero solution corresponding to an eigenvalue, for example sin(nπx/L).
An expansion of a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines of increasing frequency.
The Fourier sine expansion of a function given only on 0 < x < L, obtained by odd extension.
The weight of a particular sine or cosine term, found by integrating the data against that term.
The time-independent solution that a time-dependent problem approaches as t grows; it satisfies Laplace's equation.
The part of a solution that decays with time, leaving only the steady state.
The constant c in the wave equation, in m/s, at which each travelling disturbance moves.
The constant α² in the heat equation, in m²/s, measuring how quickly temperature differences spread.
A point of a standing wave where the displacement stays zero for all time.
The lowest-frequency separated solution, with n = 1; it decays slowest in the heat problem and has the largest period in the wave problem.
A problem whose solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the given data.
A property of harmonic functions: the largest and smallest values occur on the boundary, not inside.
